Breeze of Breslov

Parashas Vayeitzei | Nov 12th-13th 2021

G-d is Inside of You

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus 

I once had a student who suffered from tremendous internal doubts about his faith. He rarely spoke in class and it was fairly difficult to gauge what was going on inside of him. One day, he stopped showing up entirely. 

I tried reaching out to him over the course of a few weeks to see how he was doing, but he didn’t pick up his phone or respond to my messages. I continued to pray for him every day, hoping that he would find whatever it was that he was looking for. 

Purim was right around the corner, and he was still no where to be found. However, when my students put together a Purim party, he showed up unexpectedly. 

He approached me with a huge smile on his face and thanked me deeply. I never saw him smile like that. 

He proceeded to open up to me for the first time about his lifelong difficulties with believing in HaShem, as well as his more recent challenges in connecting to the teachings of Rebbe Nachman. He told me that he had essentially given up on Judaism and this was the real reason why he stopped coming to class. 

However, he felt bad about the fact that the one plan of action I advocated so strongly for, he could never push himself to do. Finally, he told me that before he gives up on HaShem completely, he felt it was only fair to follow through with Rebbe Nachman’s main piece of advice. 

One hour of Hitbodedut. 

No distraction. No interruption. 60 consecutive minutes of secluded personal conversation with the Creator of the universe, like He is your best friend (Likutey Moharan Tinyana, 25). 

My student explained that during the first 45 minutes, he felt absolutely nothing. However, in the last fifteen minutes, he started to feel an ever increasing wave of peacefulness and tranquility come over him. Finally, when he reached the 60 minute mark, he stated with tremendous enthusiasm, “For the first time in my life, I saw G-d!” 

What makes Hitbodedut the ultimate mechanism for experiencing the awesome reality of HaShem? 

Why did Rebbe Nachman so frequently “pound the table” for this unique universal practice? 

In this week’s Torah portion, “VaYeitzi”, we find the answer. 

As Yaakov Avinu was departing from his home, looking to establish his personal path in spirituality, he decided to engage in the unique practice passed down by his father and grandfather in theexact place that they had practiced it. Following a long journey to Beit El, Yaakov had his first documented session of Hitbodedut. 

Following a life changing, out of body experience, the Torah states that Yaakov entered a state of rapture and exclaimed, “HaShem is right here, and I didn’t know it!”. 

In a remarkable lesson in Likutey Moharan, Rebbe Nachman describes the mechanics of Hitbodedut and the source of its tremendous efficacy. 

When a Jew secludes himself from society and it’s external trappings, while concurrently speaking to HaShem for an extended and uninterrupted period of time, he or she experiences a psycho spiritual state of ego-dissolution (Likutey Moharan, 52).

One’s lower self, the ego, which is comprised of the powerful pursuit for temporary pleasure, the desire for external admiration, and fear of extraneous forces, melts away entirely. The “Neshama”, one’s higher, innermost self, rises to the forefront, knocking one into a powerful state of G-d consciousness previously unexperienced. 

This powerful state of self nullification known as “Bitul”, is the hallmark of the Baal Shem Tov’s novel spiritual path known as Chassidut. The Baal Shem Tov’s great grandson, Rebbe Nachman, states matter of factly that the only way to reach this genuine state of “Bitul”, is through Hitbodedut. 

My student, as his ancestor Yaakov before him, came to the same conclusion, “How awesome is this place! This is nothing other than the House of HaShem. This is the gate to Shamayim!” 

Rebbe Nachman teaches that Avraham Avinu saw Hitbodedut as a “mountain”, a challenging terrain for the courageous minority to climb. Yitzhak Avinu saw Hitbodedut as a “field”, less arduous and more accessible, but still off-limits to the majority. Yaakov Avinu however, saw Hitbodedut as a “home”, the ultimate safe space and place of inner comfort, one needed and desired equally by all. Once Hitbodedut becomes a universal practice of humanity, Jew and non-Jew alike, Rebbe Nachman states that we will be privy to the Redemption and coming of Mashiach (Likutey Moharan, 10). 

I encourage everyone to take this advice to heart and find one hour during Shabbat to pour out your heart to HaShem in your own words, like He is your best friend, and bring that state of 

Geula closer. With this you will begin to find the home you always yearned for but never truly believed existed. 

As HaShem himself states in His Torah, “Build Me a home and I will dwell in them”. 

That “home” is Hitbodedut and that dwelling space is not outside of you, it’s within you. 

Shabbat Shalom. 

“That “home” is Hitbodedut and that dwelling space is not outside of you, it’s within you.”

-Rabbi Kalmus

Eyes Open, Eyes Closed

Aaron London, BSN, RN 

Rabbi Yosef Ergas, in sefer Shomer Emunim, which serves as an introduction to Kabbalah, conveys a foundational idea related to the narratives contained within the Torah. He writes, “There is no doubt that in truth, apart from the objective that is derived from the straightforward meaning of those stories about moral behavior like all other historical accounts, there must also be a powerfully [deep] objective in the stories, to hint at great secrets and the ideas related to all the true branches of wisdom” (p. 158, from R’ Avinoam Fraenkel’s translation). 

The aforementioned point roots us in a principle we discussed in last week’s article: while the basic text is offering us insight into the stories of our Avos and Immos, a deeper reading yields insight into the dynamics that play out within our own inner worlds. Rabbi Ergas writes further, “In the end, with the entire Torah, the text talks in terms of the lower worlds [this physical world], but it hints at the supernal worlds…” (p. 164). 

As we mentioned last week based on a conversation I had with my teacher, Rabbi Gerzi, “the Ari HaKodesh in Shaar Gilgulim, Perek Aleph relates that the four spiritual universes – Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiah – exist not only in the cosmic sense as a reality outside of the self, but also in a psychological sense that exist within the self” (London, “The Chumash Within”). Therefore, if the text of the Torah “hints at the supernal worlds” and our tzaddikim teach that the supernal worlds also exist as modes of consciousness, then we can understand that the text of the Torah is inviting us to experience our Avos and Immos, not just as personalities, but as psychological modes of being as well. 

With the above introduction in mind, let us now move inwards, towards the ‘Leah’ that exists at the core of our human experience. Rabbi Y.Y. Jacobson, in his article, “Do You Know Who You Married?,” conveys the following point in regards to marriage: “‘Leah’, a name that literally means “one who is weary”, represents those elements in our spouse that are more complicated, perplexing and disturbing. Leah, the weak-eyed sister, weakened from tears and anxiety, embodies our continuous and exhausting struggle with the dark demons and ugly impulses in our lives.” 

While Rabbi Jacobson is referring to the ‘Leah’ within one’s spouse, I think it is clear that the concept of ‘Leah’ exists also within ourselves. 

The Torah characterizes Leah’s eyes as tender. Our eyes are tender as well. We also cannot stop crying. 

Rashi explains that the reason Leah could not stop crying was because “she was under the impression that she was destined to ascend to the lot of Esau” (p. 322, Artscroll translation). 

Leah was not married to Esav, and yet, the fear of the possibility was enough to have the Torah define Leah by her wearied, crying eyes. Is that not the condition of anxiety today – running away from something that is not even there? 

In the midst of our tears, Rebbe Nachman whispers to us a secret: “Close your eyes,” he says. In Torah 65 of sefer Likutey Moharan, Rebbe Nachman explains that when a person is undergoing suffering, he has to close his eyes completely from the experience of being in this world. He has to close off all external stimuli and soften into the darkness of the inner world. It is precisely that darkness which provides the possibility to see with the strong, inner eye – the eye that perceives that truly everything is from Hashem and everything Hashem does is to invite us into a more profound experience of goodness. The concealment of Hashem’s light we experience with eyes open becomes the revelation of Hashem’s light with eyes closed. Then, when we gaze at the aspect of ourselves called ‘Leah’, all the darker parts of ourselves shine with the possibility of renewed healing. 

Gut Shabbos, 

ALY 

P.S. 

A special thank you to my teacher, Rabbi Gerzi, who is generous with his time and offers insights and suggestions that are so important in the development of these pieces. Thank you, Rabbi, for helping me believe in myself. 

A special thank you to R’ Joey Rosenfeld, whose Torah informs everything I hope to share. 

A special thank you to Rabbi Kalmus, my dear friend and rabbi, who invited me into the world of Breslov and helped me to experience my portion of Rebbe Nachman’s Torah A special thank you to my wife, who always strengthens me to continue. My greatest joy is going through life with you. May you be blessed always.

“The concealment of Hashem’s light we experience with eyes open becomes the revelation of Hashem’s light with eyes closed.” 

-Aaron London

Shalom is the Highest 

Expression of Emet

Alex Aminov 

In this week’s parsha we read about Yaakov venturing out on his own. Taking his journey to find his wife, unable to return home where his bloodthirsty, twin brother Esav is ready to kill him for taking Issac’s blessing. There are many perplexing questions here. Firstly, the famous question, how could Yaakov, the tzaddik, the “ish taam”, man of simplicity do such a thing? After all, when we think of a man of holy simplicity, we would assume he’s someone who’s straightforward, never lying or attempting clever tricks. Another question that’s perplexed me is, why go through any of this in the first place? Why slight your brother and trick your father to end up impoverished and on the run when it was your blessing to receive in the first place. Why not just come up to Isaac and say, “Esav has sold me his birthright, he has no rights to it now. I am now considered your firstborn, please bless me as such.” In fact, that’s exactly the approach I’d expect from an “ish taam”, just being forthright and simple about the truth. Why go through all this? 

Well, a deeper “truth” may lie in Rav Nachman’s teachings to help shed some light on the perplexing behavior of our holy forefather. Rav Nachman explains there are different levels of truth. In our society, we were raised to believe that there’s the truth, and then there’s a lie. 

But according to chasidut, there are lies, then truths, then different ascending levels of higher truths. For example, when Rabbi Natan (Rabenu’s main student), was finally 

offered his dream job of being chief Rabbi of his town, he came to Rav Nachman for advice on whether he should take the position. Rav Nachman said, “it’s an amazing position, you’re perfectly suited for it, there’s no better fit than you, and the entire community will benefit immeasurably from you being rabbi.” This made Rabbi Natan very happy to hear, as he held Rabenu’s advice in very high regard. But then Rabbi Natan thought to himself, “Wait, Rabbi Nachman taught me that there’s the truth, then there’s the “truth of truths”. 

Rabbi Natan asked Rabbi Nachman “is that the truth?” Rabeinu responded “Yes”. Then he followed up with, “But is it the truth of truths?” Rabeinu responded: “No, the truth of truths is you will gain much more learning by me and working on writing and spreading my teachings.” 

Rabbi Natan listened to Rabbi Nachman, despite the fact that it meant walking away from his longtime dreams and desires for himself. And we’re glad he did today. Because Rabbi Nachman was right. Had he taken that position he would not have spread the teachings that have a massive global effect we see today. Millions of people, Jews and non-Jews alike benefit immeasurably from these teachings for over two centuries.

These teachings have brought people peace, emuna, tshuva, closeness with God, better relationships, and have even pulled people out of the brink of suicide. There’s the truth, then there’s the truth of truths. And what does Rabbi Nachman say is the highest level of truth? – Shalom, aka peace. It’s also one of HaShem’s names. It doesn’t just mean when there’s no war. It refers to the Kabbalistic expression of Godliness where HaShem is able to make two paradoxical opposing forces in harmony with each other. 

This means (going contrary to what many people would think), bending the truth for the sake of peace would technically be a higher truth than being outright and honest if it means I am hurting someone or making a big fight. Because there’s the truth and then there’s the truth of truths. The truth is that it was Yaakov’s birthright, he can demand it. But that means coming to his father and telling him his dear firstborn son Esav, a relationship Isaac treasures, sold his firstborn status for some soup. “That’s how much Esav values your blessing and being your firstborn.” Perhaps this would have broken Issac’s heart. But it’s the truth?! Yes, but then there’s the truth of truths, which is peace. Yaakov went against his simple nature to do something very out of character and send him running for his life but he stuck to the truth of truths. 

When Leah was put in Rachel’s place at her wedding, she was quiet. But wasn’t this supposed to be her husband? She had every right to speak up, this was a terrible injustice. That’s the truth. But the truth of truths is that it’s better to remain quiet than to embarrass her sister. And thank HaShem for Rachel remaining quiet, because Leah marries Yaakov and has Yehuda, from whom comes Moshiach. The geula of the world could rest on just one person – one time deciding to forgo the truth and seek out Shalom – the truth of truths, even if it means letting go of what we think we are owed, because HaShem wants to give us so much more.
